title: Melinda and Melinda
full_review:
Sorry to say "Melinda and Melinda" (Fox Searchlight) is not the film to change Woody Allen's unfortunate losing streak.

The premise would seem to be full of promise. Theatrical folk at a New York eatery, and two playwrights (Wallace Shawn and Larry Pine) arguing about how a basic plot can be made either comic or serious, depending on how the story is approached.

Someone at the table tells a story, though we, the viewers, don't hear it, and the writers each take turns explaining how they'd interpret the story.

In the tragic version, down-and-out Melinda (Radha Mitchell, as in the comedic interpretation) unexpectedly shows up at a dinner party thrown by her old school friend, Laurel (Chloe Sevigny), and her husband, struggling actor Lee (Jonny Lee Miller), soon identified as an alcoholic philanderer. Melinda's lost her children in a custody battle, and has tried to commit suicide. (Further dark revelations come out by the end.) Laurel tries to set her up on a blind date with a dentist, but Melinda is instead attracted to the dapper pianist and opera composer, Ellis (Chiwetel Ejiofor).

When Melinda and Ellis later take Laurel out to cheer her up after a fight with her husband, romantic sparks fly between the unhappy wife and Ellis, leading to a dramatic blowout some time later.

In the comic version, Melinda lives beneath a couple, Susan (Amanda Peet) and actor Hobie (Will Ferrell). The latter is smitten with Melinda. When Susan tries to set Melinda up with a handsome dentist (Josh Brolin), Hobie is beside himself. Later when Susan, an independent film director, is discovered in bed with another man, Hobie is overjoyed because he feels now he'll be free to pursue Melinda. But this Melinda has just hooked up with musician Billy (Daniel Sunjata), prompting Hobie to pick up another woman, the neurotic Stacey (Vinessa Shaw), which ends disastrously. And so it goes.

Among the myriad problems with Allen's screenplay is that the comic portions are scarcely funnier than the more dramatic version, and the parallel stories are only fitfully interesting. In spite of all the opening talk about the meaning of life and so forth, the material feels wafer-thin.

The dialogue is perplexingly artificial, and the back and forth between the two versions is frequently confusing. On the plus side, the performances are good and New York location shooting picturesque, in Allen's customary style.

The film contains a benevolent treatment of marital infidelity and promiscuity, sexual situations, some profanity and crude language, alcohol and drug use, and attempted suicide. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
